raw_response:
I'm 38, been farming these 5 mu in Quzhou County for 13 years now, since my father handed me the land when I was 25. It's October, time to get the winter wheat in. My farm is small — just 5 mu — so every yuan I spend has to count. My wife works at a garment factory in town and my oldest is in high school, so between me, my father who's 65 but still helps out, and my younger daughter, we handle most of the farm work ourselves. We only hire help or machinery when the timing is too tight to manage alone.

For the wheat, I'm planting the same improved variety I've used for three years now — the one my neighbor Lao Zhang recommended after he tried it first. Last year I saved my own seed but the germination wasn't great, so this year I bought fresh seed from the shop: about 10 kg per mu, costing me about 38 yuan per mu. The extension station says 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I've found my soil needs a bit more to get decent results, and honestly, last year when I cut back to save money my yield dropped more than the savings were worth. So I put down about 35 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base — the 15-15-15 type, the one in the blue bags — and then at jointing in spring I topdress with about 18 kg of urea per mu. Some of the bigger farmers down the road put down more, but with only 5 mu I can't afford to overdo it, and this amount has given me stable results. I irrigate the wheat three times: once at planting if the soil is dry, then at green-up in March, and again at jointing in April. If spring is really dry I might add one at flowering, but pumping costs about 5 yuan per mu each time, so I watch the weather and try not to waste money on water if rain is coming. For pests, I'll spray herbicide once in early spring for the weeds — the wild oats are bad in my field — and I'll keep an eye out for aphids; if they show up in April, I'll spray insecticide.

Wheat harvest is in early June, and the window is brutally tight. I always hire a combine harvester — 50 yuan per mu — because there's no way me and my father can cut 5 mu by hand in time to get the maize planted. Even with the machine, I need to be ready to plant maize within two or three days, or I miss the best window.

For summer maize, I plant right after wheat harvest around mid-June. I use a regular hybrid maize seed, not the most expensive kind, about 2.5 kg per mu at 52 yuan per mu. For fertilizer, I put about 30 kg of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and then topdress with about 15 kg of urea at the big trumpet stage. That's a bit less than what the extension agent recommends, but two years ago I tried matching his rate and didn't see enough extra yield to justify the cost, so I'd rather save those yuan. My father and I can handle the maize planting and most of the work, though if the harvest is heavy I might hire a day laborer to help haul cobs. Maize irrigation — I usually water twice, once at the V6 stage and once at tasseling if it's dry. If the summer rains are good, maybe just once. For maize pests, I spray herbicide at planting and watch for armyworms in August.

Labor-wise, wheat takes about 10 family days over the season — planting, fertilizing twice, irrigating three times, spraying, and helping with harvest transport. I hire the combine and that's about 2 hired days total. Maize takes about 8 family days, plus maybe 1 hired day if harvest is heavy and my father gets tired. I expect about 410 kg per mu of wheat and about 440 kg per mu of maize this year, assuming normal weather. Last year I got 420 kg wheat and 450 kg maize, but you never know with the weather, so I'd rather be a bit conservative. Total input costs will run about 2,230 yuan for the year. That's a big chunk for us, but with my wife's off-farm income we can manage it. I thought hard about cutting fertilizer to save money, but I learned my lesson two years ago — the yield loss hurt worse than the input cost.
